store.1: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite challenging, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses. It feels surreal to have come so far from my intro classes to now tackling complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics.
store.2: My favorite class this semester is Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by the theory behind real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or handling huge datasets efficiently. The class covers dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems, which can be mind-bending. However, our professor's intuitive explanations make these concepts more accessible. She'll present a seemingly impossible problem and then show us a strategy to approximate a solution. I always leave the class with a buzzing mind, eager to explore more.

store.4: I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is the second hardest. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project simulating a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure, as we collaborate with individuals having different coding styles and ideas about the final product. This is similar to real-world scenarios where integration and handling of concurrency issues and node failures are crucial. It can be nerve-wracking, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a bug caused by a misplaced bracket in a config file. However, once we fixed it and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is from the industry and has worked on indie games that gained traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, physics implementation, and user experience design. The assignments are super creative, and I had a blast designing a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept. The challenge was balancing the difficulty curve to avoid frustrating players. It was rewarding to see the design come together.

store.8: I'm also taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which initially intimidated me. However, the professor's approach focuses on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. We learn about linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're modeling algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing and has changed my problem-solving approach.

store.10: I'm taking a Capstone Project course, which is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface, and ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and keeping ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and agile practices. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a Philosophy of Mind class, which is my last required non-CS elective. It's interesting because it ties back into AI in some ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to analyze abstract ideas and see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could mimic or simulate human thinking. I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for that perspective.

store.14: My typical college schedule is quite packed. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are slightly lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be challenging if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it adds to the workload.

The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can be even more time-consuming if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time commitment. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a logistical nightmare. However, despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment.
